1.43.m: Pulastya said: / There appeared a doorkeeper clad in white Chinese silk. / Falling to the earth on his knees and covering his mouth with his hand,
he spoke a clear speech refined with few syllables / to the Daitya lord, who possessed a radiant body resembling a cluster of suns:
"Kālanemi, having bound the gods, has presented them and stands at the gate. / He inquires: 'Where should the crowd of captives be kept, O Lord?'"
Hearing those words of the doorkeeper, the Daitya said: / "Let them stay wherever they wish; the three worlds are my house.
Only Vāsava alone should be released after having his head shaved, / wrapped in a white cloth, and branded with a dog's foot."
When this was done, the gods, with aching hearts, / went to see the lotus-born [Brahmā], teacher of the world, for refuge.
Despondent, having approached him and touched the ground with their heads, / they praised the lotus-seated one with words rich in fine syllables.

The gods said: / "Homage to you, the source beginning from the sprout of Oṃkāra, prior to the endless division of world-abodes! / To you who arose thereafter, the root of sattva, desiring destruction—homage to you whose form is sattva!"

Contemplating you as the primordial source of manifest beings, and from that renown which is our name, / you made the division of heaven and earth, of the upper worlds, and likewise below from this cosmic egg.
Clearly Meru became your chorion; thus we know that space was fashioned by you. / Clearly the gods were born from your body, within whose body embodied beings move.

Heaven is your head; the moon and sun are your eyes; serpents are your hair; the quarters of space are your ear-cavities; / the sacrifice is your body; the rivers are your joints; the earth is your feet; and the oceans are your belly.

You are celebrated as the creator of illusion, the cause, peaceful according to the Vedas, the light, the sun; / through the meaning of the Vedas, with the intellect, they reveal you, the ancient one, abiding within the lotus of the heart.

Those who have attained yoga proclaim you the self; those seven subtle principles set forth by the Sāṃkhyas, / and that eighth which is sung as their cause—dwelling within them as the living soul, you alone are that.

Having beheld your gross and subtle form, whichever entities have been declared in the causal state, / they indeed arose from you alone at the primordial creation; at the end of mental impressions, they must merge back into you.

Your appointed sign is deep within the inner womb; time, whose divisions and doubts have been destroyed, / is the cause of being, non-being, the unmanifest, and dissolution; endless is it, and you are its maker and foundation.

All that is gross is worthless; distinct from it is that subtle reality which is sung as superior even to them. / And by whom the gross entities are pervaded, grosser than them you are declared in the Purāṇa.

You unite every prosperous being with its entity, conceived within each feeling; / casting away what is joined through manifestation, you establish the functioning of manifestation in its proper place.
Thus the god is the refuge of manifest beings, the savior, the protector, meditated upon as having an endless form. / Having thus praised Brahmā the cause, the immortals fell silent.
Then they stood, praying in their minds for the attainment of their desired object. / Praised in this manner, Viriñci became exceedingly pleased.
Giver of boons though he was, he spoke to the immortals, pointing with his left hand. / Brahmā said: "Like a woman whose husband is alive yet she has cast off bracelets from her hands,
why do you not shine, Śakra, with your withered lotus-face? / Fire, even though separated from smoke, you do not shine;
covered by a heap of grass, like a forest fire extinguished long ago! / Yama, tormented by an afflicted body, you do not shine today,
dragged at every step as if relying upon your staff for support! / Lord of the night-roamers, why do you speak as if terrified?
You appear as if wounded by the enemy in the attack mounted by the lord of the Rākṣasas. / Varuṇa, your body is dried up, as if enveloped by fire;
behold your realm, devoid of water! / Vāyu, you are bewildered, as if pierced by the tips of swords!
Dhanada, why are you bowed down, as if abandoning your status as Kubera? / Rudras, though bearing tridents, where has your great valor vanished?
By whom has the fierce power of you all been struck down? Let that be told!" / Having been addressed thus by that Brahmā who abides in the Brahman,
the gods, since he is the foremost in speech, impelled the wind. / Then the wind, urged on by the gods headed by Śakra,
said to the four-faced god: "You know all that moves and is still. / The immortals headed by Purahūta, together with their armies, were forcibly conquered by hundreds of Daityas.

Sacrifices of wondrous and diverse qualities have been established by you for the maintenance of the worlds; / and the performative sages who attain the desired fruits taught in revelation were established from you alone in the beginning.

Indeed heaven belonged to the eaters of the sacrifice constantly by virtue of your appointment; / having seized the host of aerial chariots, it was made by that Danu's son into a ground for his great elephants.
You who made that mountain, possessing all superior qualities as the king of all mountains, / the mountain abode of the gods adorning sacrifices, the limit of the luminous bodies in the sky—
its slopes and peaks, suitable for dwelling and sport, have been adorned by the Danava; / its multitude of hanging gem-filled caves has been reduced to an abode for many Daityas.
And out of fear of that Asura, through having a despondent body, / that face of the quarters filled with spotless radiance has been seized to be enjoyed by him for a very long time.

Even the thunderbolt, the best of the gods' weapons fashioned by you in the first cosmic age, / having struck the body of Diti's son, shattered into a hundred pieces like the conflicting thoughts of an ignorant man.

With limbs pierced in battle by arrows, shown in by the doorkeepers at the gate, / we gained entry with difficulty to that enemy of the immortals.
The gods were dragged into the assembly, O lord, and forced to sit; / not speaking, they were mocked by others who carried canes in their hands:
"You men of great purpose, who have accomplished all aims, speak little; / speak now in accordance with the treatises, immortals who talk so much!
This is the assembly of the lion among Daityas, not the unruly assembly of Śakra!" / Thus speaking, the servants of the Daitya laughed at us greatly.
And the seasons in embodied form attend upon him day and night; / having committed an offense, terrified, they never leave him by any means.
Accompanied by the lute, tempo, and melody, by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, / passionate music conforming to style is sung in his mansions.
He weighs friends and others with slight or heavy regard according to services rendered or unrendered; / he abandons those who come for refuge and has cast off the haven of truth.
Thus completely—or rather, by whom can his insolence / be recounted without remainder? The Creator is the ultimate resort in that matter.
Having said this, Vāyu slowly ceased from [telling] the gods' doings. / Then the Lord, with a lotus face bearing a smile, spoke to the gods:
Brahmā said: / "The Daitya Tāraka cannot be slain by all the gods and Asuras; / the man who can slay him is not yet born in the three worlds.
Gratifying him with the grant of a boon, he was turned away by me / from his austerity—a king whose very nature now burns the three worlds.
That Daitya, however, chose death from an infant seven days old; / and that seven-day-old child will be born from Śaṃkara.
He will be the slayer of Tāraka, radiant like the sun. / At present, the lord, the blessed Śaṃkara, is without a wife.
She who will become the daughter of the Himālaya, the goddess, / from her shall come a son, like fire from a fire-stick;
having begotten him, when he is reached, Tāraka will cease to be. / The means has been declared by me how this shall surely happen.
Divide among yourselves the remainder of his power immediately thereafter; / wait for a short time with an undaunted heart."
Thus addressed by that lotus-born [creator] himself, / those thirty gods, sky-dwellers, bowed down to the lord and departed as was fitting.
Then, when the gods had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, / the blessed one, remembered Night, that goddess born of old.

Then the blessed Night approached the grandfather; / seeing that Night in solitude, Brahmā said:

Brahmā said: / O Night, a great task for the gods is at hand; / you must accomplish it, O goddess; hear the decision regarding this task.
There is a lord of Daityas named Tāraka, an unconquered enemy of the gods; / for his destruction, the blessed Lord [Śiva] will bring forth [a son].
That son will indeed be the destroyer of that Tāraka. / She who was the wife of Śaṅkara, Satī, daughter of Dakṣa,
She, the goddess, having become angry at her father for a certain reason, / will be born as the daughter of the snowy mountain, bringing welfare to the world.
Hara, considering the three worlds empty due to separation from her, / will reside for some time in a cave of that snowy mountain frequented by Siddhas,
awaiting her birth. / The great son born to the two of them, who will have performed severe austerities,
will become the destroyer of that Daitya Tāraka. / And as soon as she is born, that goddess, a radiant maiden with mere slumbering consciousness,
deeply longing in separation, eager for union with Hara— / the union of the two, who will have performed severe austerities, will bring auspiciousness.
Then, however, a slight verbal quarrel will arise between the two; / then, once more, doubt is seen regarding [the slaying of] Tāraka.
Therefore, when the two are united, you must cause an obstacle / to the cause of their sexual union; listen to how [it must be done] by both of them.
while in the womb of her mother, with your own form and name— / then Śarva, laughing at her playfully, crestfallen,
will mock that goddess; then she, infuriated, / will go away to perform austerities; then, endowed with austerities,
she will bear from Śarva that [son of] boundless circle of radiance. / He will indeed become the slayer of the enemies of the gods, without doubt.
by you also, O goddess, the Dānavas unconquerable by the world must be slain, / until, O ruler of the gods, her body gathers an accumulation of virtues,
so long, through her union, will you not be able to slay the Daityas. / When this is done, having performed austerities, she will accomplish everything with you.
When, O goddess, Umā shall have completed her observances, / then that daughter of the mountain shall attain her own natural form.
Then she, Bhavānī, will be united with you; / and you, joined with a portion of her form, will become [an aspect] of Umā.
The world will worship you as Ekānaṃśā, O bestower of boons, / as all-pervading and fulfilling desires under various forms and distinctions.
[You are] the Gāyatrī whose face is the syllable Oṃ by those who expound Brahman; / by kings of mighty arms, when overwhelmed, [you are revered as] having a powerful form;
you are the earth, the mother of the Vaiśyas; by Śūdras you are worshipped as Śaivī; / [you are] the unshakeable patience of sages, and the compassion of the self-restrained;
you are the doubt in great stratagems; policy for those who practice statecraft; / you are the comprehension of objectives; you are the yearning residing in the heart of living beings;
you are liberation for all beings; you are the destination of all embodied souls; / you are pleasure for those whose minds seek pleasure; you are affection in the heart of embodied beings;
you are fame for the truthful; you are tranquility for those of wicked deeds; / you are delusion for all beings; you are the destination for those who offer sacrifices;
you are the great shore of the oceans, and the sportive, playful woman; / you are the night that grants the joy of embracing the neck of the beloved.
Thus in manifold forms you are worshipped in the world, O goddess! / Those who shall praise you, O granter of boons, and those who shall worship you—
they will attain all their desires, without a doubt. / Thus addressed, the goddess Night, folding her hands and saying, "So be it,"
went swiftly at once to the great palace of the Snow Mountain. / There she saw Menā seated in a great mansion, resting against a jeweled wall,
the lotus of her face pale in complexion, / somewhat slender, weighed down by the rising burden of her breasts.
protected by a host of potent herbs and royal mantras, / charming with an amulet worn bound with gold to protect the life [of the unborn child],
illuminated by the vast light from clusters of jeweled lamps, / where many white mustard seeds were scattered and charming attendants [were present],
radiant with an awning of pure Chinese silk and carpets covering the floor, / delightful with the fragrance of incense, with all useful items prepared.
Then, as the day gradually departed far away, the night / brought forth pleasant awakenings; then, in the great house of Menā,
when people were mostly asleep, slumber having made its approach, / the moon shining clearly, and night-birds fluttering,
the courtyards covered by spirits moving about in the night, / and the handsome folk locked in close embraces around the neck,
the pair of lotus eyes of Menā having attained a slight weariness, / Night, of marvelous union, entered her mouth with ease.
Then indeed, to cause the maddening ecstasy of the mother of the universe, / she entered the interior of her womb by degrees, considering it an incomparable birth.
the night adorned the goddess's house like a fire-stick of Guha; / then, the cause of liberation for the world, the beloved of the Snow Mountain,
in the auspicious hour of Brahmā, gave birth to the fire-stick of Guha. / And when she was born, the creatures, both stationary and moving,
all became happy, all the inhabitants of the worlds; / even for the inhabitants of hell there was then great happiness equal to heaven;
the mind of cruel creatures became calm, and so did that of embodied beings; / the radiance of the celestial bodies became even brighter then;
and the herbs growing in the forest became sapful and the fruits [delicious]; / garlands became fragrant, and the sky became spotless;
and the wind of pleasant touch, and the quarters highly delightful, / radiant with the quality of the ripening of the fruits produced by the seasons—
the earth-goddess became crowded with garlands of rice-plants, / and the long-practiced austerities of the purified sages [bore fruit];
reached fruition at that time for those of spotless minds; / and the forgotten scriptures manifested themselves anew;
the power of the principal holy bathing-places was most sacred then; / and in the sky, gods were present in thousands of aerial cars.
Headed by the great Indra, the lord of waters, the wind, and fire, / they released a shower of flowers upon that snowy mountain.
the foremost Gandharvas sang, and troops of Apsarases danced; / even the great mountains, Meru and the rest, assumed embodied forms;
divine beings with outstretched hands, when that great festival had arrived, / and oceans and rivers arrived from all directions.
The snowy mountain, the best of mountains, was then to be served, / approached, and sought as refuge by all moving and unmoving beings in the world.
having experienced the festival, the gods then departed to their own abodes, / accompanied by crowds of sportive gods, nāga-chiefs, Gandharvas, and mountains.
competing with one another, the goddess, the daughter of the snowy mountain, / was gradually brought to discernment and learning by unwearied wise ones.
Gradually, through beauty, good fortune, and awakening in the three worlds, / the daughter of the Himālaya came to possess all auspicious marks.
In the meantime, Śakra, intent on accomplishing his objective, / then remembered the celestial sage Nārada, who is esteemed by the gods.
Knowing the desire of Śakra, the lord [Nārada] then / came with joy to the dwelling of the great Indra.
Seeing him, the thousand-eyed Vāsava rose from his great seat / and worshipped him with water for the feet, as was fitting.
Having duly received the worship offered by Śakra, / Nārada inquired about the welfare of the god who subdued Pāka.
And when asked about his welfare, the powerful Śakra spoke these words: / Indra said: 'A sprout of welfare has indeed arisen in the three worlds;
"Upon the accomplishment of the fruit of that, you are known by me, O sage; / indeed, you know all that, yet you are urged forward [by me].
one attains supreme satisfaction upon disclosing a matter to a friend: / [it is] that the mountain-born goddess may attain union with the Bearer of the Bow.'
Let an effort quickly be made in this way by all who belong to our side." / Understanding the entire matter, Nārada then took his leave,
and the lord quickly went to the abode of the Snow Mountain. / There at the gate, crowded with various cane-rods, that best of brāhmaṇas
was saluted by the Snow Mountain, who came out before him. / Entering together the dwelling that had become an ornament of the earth,
the eminent sage of matchless radiance sat down on a great seat, / spacious and golden, offered by the Snow Mountain himself.
The mountain offered him guest-water and foot-water as was fitting; / the sage then accepted that guest-water according to the rules.
Having accepted the guest-water, the mountain, with his lotus-face gently blooming, / inquired in a soft voice after the well-being of the great sage's austerities.
The sage too then asked after the well-being of the king of mountains. / Nārada said: "Ah, O great mountain, your dwelling is suitable for dharma!
O sinless one, the breadth of your caves is equal to the mind; / the weight of your abundant virtues surpasses [other] immovable things.
The clarity of your water surpasses even that of sages; / we do not perceive, O lord of mountains, where any lack of restraint can reside.
By sages of diverse austerities, radiant like fire and the sun, / who dwell in your caves, you are constantly purified as a sacred place.
Disdaining celestial chariots, detached from dwelling in heaven, / gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras dwell [here] as in their father's house.
Ah, blessed are you, O lord of mountains, in whose cave Hara, / the lord of the world, resides, devoted to meditation upon Rāma!"
When the divine sage Nārada had spoken thus with respectful speech, / Menā, the queen of the snow-mountain, desiring to see the sage,
followed by her daughter and accompanied by a few maidservants, / her body bent with bashfulness and affection, entered the abode
where the best of sages, self-controlled, was seated with the mountain. / Then, seeing that sage, a mass of splendour, the mountain's beloved
saluted him with veiled face, joining her lotus-palms in reverence. / Seeing that noble lady, the celestial sage of boundless radiance
magnified her with blessings that resembled the gushing of nectar. / Then, her heart filled with wonder, the daughter of the Himavat mountain,
the queen beheld Nārada, the sage of wondrous form. / And she was addressed by the sage with affectionate words: "Come, child!"
she clasped her father by the neck and sat upon his lap. / The mother said to the goddess: "Pay homage, O daughter,
to the lord rich in austerities; you will obtain an agreeable husband." / Thus addressed by her mother, she covered her face with her garment,
shook her head a little, and did not speak any word. / Then the mother spoke these words again to her daughter at that time:
"Child, salute the celestial sage, and then I will give you / an auspicious, charming jeweled toy that has been kept by me for a long time."
Thus spoken to, she then quickly rose, went up, and bowed to his feet, / placing the lotus-bud of her hands upon her head.
When the homage was performed, the mother, through the mouth of a friend, / gently prompted [the sage] to reveal her good fortune,
out of curiosity to know her bodily marks, / bearing in her heart, from a woman's nature, anxiety for her own daughter.
The mountain, understanding that gesture in the heart of his queen, / though his form showed no outward sign, considered this arrival pleasing.
Prompted then by the friend of the mountain's queen, the best of sages, / the illustrious Nārada, with a smile on his face, spoke these words:
"A husband for her is not [yet] born, O gentle lady, and he is devoid of auspicious marks; / she will always have outstretched hands and wandering feet;
she will be of beautiful complexion—what more need be said in detail?" / Hearing this, overcome with agitation, his fortitude shattered,
the great mountain Himācala, his throat choked with tears, replied to Nārada: / Himavat said: "Since the course of this worldly existence, so full of faults, is hard to comprehend,
and by the inevitable creation instituted by some supreme creator, / this order is established for worldly beings:
he who is born indeed from a seed serves the purpose of the begetter; / and yet clearly, no one belongs to the one who is born.
By their own karma alone the various kinds of living beings are born: / one born from an egg might be born again as a human;
even a human, in the crawling state, is born with human nature; / and even there, in a superior birth, by the elevation of dharma,
the remaining living beings are situated without the birth of sons; / among them, human beings in particular possess the same dharma according to moral law.
The attainment of the stages of life comes in sequence after the vow of a student, / by the ordinance of that Creator by whom worldly existence has been increased.
For there would be no generation of worldly existence if all were without households. / Moreover, the obtaining of a son is always praised by the Creator in the treatises.
For the delusion of living beings and for the sake of saving from hell, / creation devoid of woman is not possible for creatures.
The female race is indeed wretched by its very nature, having a share in misery; / through the capacity of reflection upon the treatises, [their nature] has been censured in them by the Creator.
And by Brahmā it is said repeatedly in the treatises, undoubtedly with great significance, / that she should not be knower of a superior state.
‘A daughter is equal to ten sons, even if she lacks good conduct’— / this statement has lost its fruit, a fruit that causes depression to men.
For a daughter is wretched, pitiable, the increaser of a father’s grief, / even if she has all desires fulfilled and is endowed with husband and sons.
How much more so if she is unfortunate, bereft of husband, sons, wealth, and the like! / And you have spoken of an assemblage of defects in my daughter’s body.
Alas, I am bewildered, I dry up, I languish, I sink down, O Nārada! / Even that which is unfitting and even that which is unattainable must be spoken now.
For my sake, cut away this sorrow centered on a daughter, O sage! / Although [matters are] determined beyond doubt, the mind, resorting to distress,
thirst robs what is expert, resorting again to greed for the fruit. / For the supreme birth of women, belonging to both families,
is said to be for happiness in this world and the next, called the attainment of a good husband. / Truly, because of the rarity of a good [husband], even a husband devoid of virtues
is never obtained by a woman without merits; / for dharma is without expedients, its delight arising from its final outcome.
A woman's wealth throughout her life is established in her husband. / Though penniless, foul-mouthed, foolish, and bereft of all auspicious marks,
a husband is always said to be the supreme deity of a woman. / It was said by you, the divine sage: ‘Truly, her husband is not born.’
This is incomparable, immeasurable, and intolerable misfortune; / that anxiety pervades throughout the moving and unmoving creation, O sage.
Hearing that ‘he is not born,’ this mind of mine is troubled. / A bodily mark, indicating the auspicious and inauspicious of human and divine species,
is indeed ordained by the hands and feet. / And this one, her hand upturned, has been described by you, O best of sages.
The condition of having an upturned hand is constantly spoken of as begging; / never is it of those of auspicious rising, the blessed, who give.
By you her feet were spoken of as having fair shadows, errant; / even there, O sage, no better hope appears to us.
And there are other bodily marks indicating various fruits.” / When the mountain, pondering great sorrow, ceased after saying this,
Nārada, worshipped by the gods, said this with a smile: / Nārada said: “In a circumstance of great joy, sorrow is expressed by you.
The meaning of my words was not discerned; you fall into delusion, O great mountain. / Hear this speech from me, established in secret truth.
Attentive, O great mountain, consider what was spoken by me: / When it was said by me, O Himācala, ‘The husband of this goddess is not born,’
Mahādeva is unborn, the origin of past, future, and present, / the refuge, the eternal, the ruler, Śaṃkara, the supreme lord.
Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the sages are afflicted by the womb, birth, and old age; / they are all playthings of that supreme lord, O mountain.
From the cosmic egg, by his will, the Lord of the worlds came into being; / there is no destruction of the self, O mountain, even down to the immovable.
Of the embodied being taking birth and dying in worldly existence, / only the body is destroyed here; destruction of the self is not spoken of.
This worldly existence, celebrated from Brahmā down to the immovable, / afflicted by the sorrow of birth and death, revolves day and night.
Mahādeva is immovable, motionless, unborn, the progenitor, free of old age; / he, the lord of the universe, free of illness, will be her husband.
And as for what was said by me, ‘Your goddess is bereft of marks,’ / hear properly the examination of that statement as well.
A bodily mark is indeed a divine sign, resting on parts of the body; / and it reveals the maturation of lifespan, wealth, and good fortune.
For infinite, immeasurable good fortune, however, O mountain, / no sign in the form of a mark is ordained on the body.
Therefore, O wise one, there is no bodily mark on her limbs, O mountain. / And as for what I said of her, ‘Her hand is ever upturned’—
this hand of the goddess is ever upturned as boon-granting; / she will be the granter of boons to the multitudes of gods, asuras, and sages.
And as for what was spoken by me, ‘Her feet have fair shadows, errant’— / hear from me the explanatory statement of this as well, O best of mountains.
Her two feet, resembling lotuses, are pure, radiant with nails; / by the luster of the crest jewels of bowing gods and asuras,
which have diverse colors, her feet are beheld as having fair shadows, reflected. / She is the wife of the maintainer of the universe, the bull-bannered one, O mountain;
she is the mother of all the world, who has arisen to bring about the future of beings. / Auspicious, this one of purifying radiance [is born] in your region solely for sanctification.
Therefore, O best of lordly mountains, let it be arranged by you according to rite / that she should quickly attain union with the wielder of the Pināka.
For there is a great purpose of the gods here, O snow mountain.” / Having heard all this from Nārada, the lord of mountains,
Menā's husband, considered himself born anew; / and then, overjoyed, Himācala spoke to Nārada:
“I have been lifted up by you from terrible, impassable hell, O Lord; / having raised me up from Pātāla, I have been made sovereign of the seven worlds.
Renowned as Himācala now by you, O best of sages, / I have been brought to an elevation a hundredfold greater than Himācala.
From very joy, my heart has been seized, O great sage; / it cannot determine the careful deliberation of duties.
The sight of persons like you, O sage, is certainly never in vain; / by you indeed [this realm] was spoken of as a residence for self-realized beings.
I myself have produced impurity for sages and deities; / nevertheless, let an instruction be given to me in this one matter.”
When the lord of mountains had spoken thus, Nārada, filled with great joy, / then spoke these words: "Everything has been accomplished, O lord!"
That which is for the business of the gods is an even greater concern for you as well.” / Having spoken thus, Nārada then went swiftly to the heavenly world.
Having gone to the abode of the gods, he saw Mahendra; / then the sage sat upon a great seat suitable [for him].
Questioned by Śakra, he related the story regarding the daughter of the mountain: / Nārada said: “What was told to me as my duty, that has indeed been done by me.
However, his coming within range of the arrows of the five-arrowed one is expected.” / Thus spoken to by the sage who sees purposes, the king of the gods,
the blessed Pākaśāsana, remembered the mango-blossom weapon; / remembered then quickly by the wise thousand-eyed one,
the fish-bannered one appeared with Rati, full of playful charm. / Seeing him manifest, Śakra spoke to Manmatha:
Śakra said: “What need is there of much instruction to you, beloved of Rati? / You are mind-born; therefore you know what has entered the minds of beings.
Therefore, do what is pleasing to the dwellers of heaven in due order; / quickly unite Śaṃkara with the daughter of the mountain, O mind-born one!”
"Go accompanied by this Spring, having him as your ally with Rati." / Having been addressed thus by Śakra for the accomplishment of his own purpose,
the five-arrowed god then spoke, afraid, this word to Śatakratu: / Kāma said: / "With this equipment of gods, terrifying even to sages and Dānavas,
lord Śaṅkara is difficult to subdue; do you not know this, O Lord of the world? / Do you know that this god is the primal cause, the imperishable state?
Generally, in grace as well as in wrath, everything of the great is great. / Truly, beauty originating in heaven is the essence of all enjoyments;
for those seeking something special, O Śakra, there is a fall even from common fruit." / Having heard this speech, Śakra, accompanied by the gods, said to him:
Śakra said: / "We are your authority in that matter, O beloved of Rati, without a doubt. / Without tongs, the capacity of a blacksmith is not acknowledged;
someone's competence is seen in some particular place, but not everywhere." / Having been spoken to thus, Kāma departed, having recourse to his friend Madhu.
Joined by Rati, he went quickly to the plateau of the Snow Mountain. / And having reached it, he pondered over the task, preceded by the means:
"Great souls are indeed unshakeable, their mind exceedingly difficult to conquer. / Only by first agitating it can victory over him be achieved—not otherwise.
Success generally follows when the mind has first been purified. / How can such states arise without pursuing enmity?
Wrath arises from harsher association; jealousy is a terrifying, great companion. / By fickleness, she is exceedingly strong, having shattered the receptacle of patience on the head.
I shall first introduce the dark transformation of his mind, / closing the doors of steadfastness and driving away contentment.
Indeed, no wise man here can comprehend me, / an existence born only of thought, arising in the mind of the odd-eyed god.
Having entered, undertaking action, difficult to cross like a deep whirlpool, / I shall overpower Hara, who is established in penance and firm of soul."
Covering the collection of senses, having made arrangements of charming devices, / and having reflected thus, Madana [went to] the hermitage of the Lord of beings.
He went to the essence of the earth, having altars around straight trees, / crowded with peaceful animals, unshakeable, teeming with living beings,
with clusters of various flowering creepers, with leaders of the hosts standing on its peaks, / resounded by unperturbed bulls, with slopes covered in dark green grass.
There he saw a charming second self of the three-eyed god, / Vīraka, the lord of the world of heroes, whose radiance was like that of Īśāna,
with a mass of matted hair tawny like a heap of ripe saffron filaments, / cane in hand, calm, formidable, adorned with inauspicious ornaments.
Then [he saw Śaṅkara], his eyes like the tips of partially closed, blooming lotus petals, / gazing straight ahead, fixed upon the tip of the bridge of his nose,
with a very lovely upper garment of lion's skin hanging down, / tawny from the fire of breaths released by the hoods of the serpents on his ears,
with a hanging mass of matted hair kissing the edges of his trembling cheeks, / with hands placed at the root of his navel, with Vāsuki resting around,
with snake-ornaments fastened to the tip of his nose, seated in the brahmāñjali posture; / having gradually approached near, Kāma slowly saw Śaṅkara.
Then Madana, taking support from the buzzing of bees following the trees on the slopes, / entered through the ear-hole into the mind of Bhava.
Hearing that sweet [sound] which was the abode of love, Śaṅkara / then remembered the daughter of Dakṣa, his beloved, his mind eager to sport.
Then, having slowly vanished, Śiva's meditation of concentration, / exceedingly spotless, stood before him in an object of perception.
Then, having attained absorption in that, his heart obstructed by an impediment, / the lord of the gods entered into an alteration whose nature was passion.
Slightly entered by anger, Dhūrjaṭi took hold of his steadfastness, / having expelled Madana, he remained enveloped in yogamāyā.
Entered by that māyā, Madana then blazed forth; / having a body made of desire, unfathomable, an abode of fault, high-minded.
Having emerged from the heart, he, consisting of the passion of latent impressions, / having reached the external ground, the fish-bannered god stood nearby.
Accompanied indeed for assistance by his friend Madhu, / seeing a delightful cluster of mango flowers shaken by the gentle breeze,
Madana, the crocodile-bannered god, quickly released upon Hara's chest / the arrow named Mohana.
That great, celebrated arrow fell upon his pure heart— / the harsh, tall flower-arrow that produces delusion.
Then, when the collection of sense organs was pierced in his heart, Bhava, / though the protector of beings and steadfast, became inclined toward love.
Then, through the power of his emotions, he perceived his own possession, / and he spoke many words that gave rise to obstacles.
Then, in his face made terrifying by the dread roar produced by the fire of wrath, / the third eye became agitated with fire,
terrible with the destruction of the world, belonging to Rudra of wrathful form; / Dhūrjaṭi opened it wide while Madana was standing near him.
By the spark of that eye, while the dwellers of heaven cried out, / Kandarpa, the proud inspirer of desire, was swiftly reduced to ashes.
And having reduced him to ashes, that fire born from Hara's eye / flared up to burn the world, recognizing the voracious roar.
Then Bhava, for the sake of the world, divided the fire / among the mango tree, spring, the moon, flowers, and others,
and divided the fire of love among bees and the mouth of the cuckoo; / then Hara, pierced externally and internally by the arrows of love,
beholding that fire resting divided among these parts, / which causes turmoil in the world and whose expansion is irresistible,
indeed, with his heart burning day and night with desire full of love to attain her, / the formidable [lord] came under the sway of sorrow.
Having seen Smara reduced to ashes by the flame of Hara's roar, / Rati wailed bitterly along with her friend Madhu.
Then, having lamented profusely and consoled by Madhu, / she sought refuge with the god who has the moon on his crest and three eyes.
Holding a flowering creeper born of a mango tree, followed by bees, / covered with leafy trees, become a friend to the cuckoos,
and tying up her matted hair with curly locks, / Rati, having smeared her body with the white, pleasing ashes of Smara,
fell on her knees to the ground and addressed the moon-adorned lord. / Rati said: / "Homage be to Śiva, who consists of mind, who consists of the universe, whose path is wondrous! Homage!
Homage be to Śiva, worshipped by gods, to you who are always intent on mercy toward devotees! / Homage be to Bhava, the source of existence! Homage to you, the destroyer of Madana!
Homage be to the refuge of māyā and love! Homage to the one naturally adorned with purity! / Homage be to you, immeasurable, the abode of virtues! Homage to you, the ancient perfected one!
Homage to the refuge! Homage to virtue! Homage to you, followed by terrible hosts! / Homage to the maker of prosperity in manifold worlds! Homage to the granter of desires to devotees!
Homage to the originator of action! Homage always to you of infinite forms, at all times! / To you of unendurable wrath at all times, to you marked by the moon, homage be to you!
To the one praised as supreme in boundless play, who rides the king of bulls, the destroyer of the cities, / homage to the famous, great healing medicine! Homage to you of multiform appearance!"

Praise be to Time! Praise to the minute division of time! Praise to you who transcend time and its divisions! / The best teacher to be reflected upon by the teachers of all moving and unmoving things, who envisioned the creation of beings,
I, O moon-crested one, have taken refuge in you, the Great Lord, in order to quickly regain my beloved. / Grant me, O lord, this abundance of fame; without that husband, I cannot live!

He is the beloved of his beloved, the eternal lord of men; who else is greater than him here in the worlds? / He is the master, the powerful one, the source of dear ones, skilled, paramount, the supreme burner of foes.

You alone are the protector and guardian of the world, compassionate, who uproots fear in your devotees.” / When Śaṅkara, bearing the moon upon his head, the boar-monkey, was praised thus by the beloved of the Mind-born,
the bearer of the crescent moon was pleased, and looking gently upon her, spoke. / Śaṅkara said: / “In time, O lovely one, after a long period, this Kāma will come to be.
He will become well-renowned throughout the worlds as Ananga, the Bodiless.” / Addressed thus, the beloved of Kāma bowed her head to the Lord of the Mountain,
and Rati went to another grove on the snow-covered mountain. / Miserable, she wept profusely at various delightful spots.
Though resolved to die, she turned away from death by the command of Śiva. / Then, impelled by the words of Nārada, the snow-mountain,
taking his daughter, adorned with ornaments, with auspicious festive rites performed, / wearing a wreath fashioned from heavenly flowers, and dressed in bright garments of Chinese silk,
accompanied by two female companions, the Mountain then set forth, / his heart fulfilled at that auspicious planetary alignment.
Traversing through forests, woods, and groves, / he beheld a weeping woman of inconceivable and immense splendour.
None of such beauty existed in the world upon the delightful slopes of the woods. / Struck with astonishment upon seeing her weeping, the Mountain
approached near to her and asked: / Himavat said: / “Who are you? Whose are you, auspicious lady? And why are you weeping?
I do not deem this cause to be small, O beauty of the world!” / Hearing his words, she, along with the season of Spring,
weeping and sighing words of sorrow that intensified her misery, spoke: / Rati said: / “Know me to be Rati, the cherished wife of Kāma, O you of noble vows!
On this mountain, the blessed Giriśa was engaged in ascetic practice. / Angered by the obstacle caused by him, opening his eye in rage,
and letting loose a blazing flame of fire, he reduced Kāma to mere ashes. / Terrified and agitated, I went for refuge to that god,
and praised him; then Giriśa, well pleased, spoke to me: / ‘I am pleased, O beloved of Kāma; Kāma will indeed be born again.
And a man who recites this praise of yours with devotion, relying upon me, / shall attain his desired wish; turn away, therefore, from death!’
Awaiting his word, under the sway of hope, / I shall preserve this body for some time, O one of great splendour.”
Thus spoken to by that Rati, the mountain, formidable in his agitation, / took his daughter by the hand and wished to go to his own city.
Because what is destined inevitably occurs, she who was to become the mother of beings, / feeling shy, spoke to her father, the Mountain, through the mouths of her female companions.
The Mountain’s daughter said: / “What purpose have I with this unfortunate body? / And how can Śaṅkara, having reached such a state, become my husband?
One’s desire is attained through austerities; nothing is unattainable for one who practices asceticism. / To be unfortunate in the world is in vain when the means is at hand.
Free from doubt regarding asceticism, wishing to achieve my own goal, / I shall perform severe austerities; I am leaving.” When his daughter spoke thus,
the lord of mountains spoke with a voice choked with emotion: / Himavat said: / “O child, U mā! It is rash! Your body is not capable
of enduring austerities commensurate with such suffering, O gentle-faced one! / Things that are destined to happen are ever accomplished;
destined events come to pass in abundance even for one who does not desire them. / Therefore, young girl, there is no need for you to perform austerities.
Let us go to our abode; I shall deliberate there.” / But when, addressed thus, the daughter of the mountain would not follow him home,
the Mountain, seized with anxiety, praised his own daughter. / Then a divine voice echoed in the sky throughout the three worlds:
“Because you said to your daughter, ‘U mā! O daughter, it is rash!’, / her name shall therefore be Umā throughout the worlds.
She is perfection embodied; she will accomplish what has been conceived.” / Hearing that voice in the vault of heaven,
the Mountain granted permission to his daughter and quickly went to his own abode. / Pulastya said: / The daughter of the mountain also went to the mountain inaccessible even to the gods.
Followed by her two female companions, the daughter of the king of mountains, firmly resolved, [went to] / the holy peak of Himavat, adorned with various minerals,
overspread with divine flowering creepers, its trees resounding with bees, / endowed with celestial springs, radiant with hundreds of desires,
filled with various birds, graced by cakravāka geese, / adorned with sacred, blossoming flowers born of water and land,
sheltering wondrous caves, furnished with divine dwellings, / resounding with flocks of birds, crowded with wish-yielding trees.
There they saw a tree with great boughs and green foliage, / endowed with blossoms of all seasons, graced by cakravākas,
covered with hundreds of diverse flowers, bearing various kinds of fruits, / untouched by the rays of the sun, with dense, spreading sprouts.
Casting aside her garments and ornaments there, the daughter of the mountain / was wrapped in divine bark-garments, wearing a girdle made of darbha grass.
Bathing thrice daily and subsisting on pāṭalā flowers, she spent a hundred autumns. / Then for a hundred [years] she sustained herself on a single withered leaf.
She, the treasure of asceticism, remained completely without food for a hundred years. / Then all living beings were distressed by the fire of her ascetic power.
Then the blessed lord of a hundred sacrifices remembered the Seven Sages. / Having arrived, delighted and assembled together,
honoured by Mahendra, they asked him of his purpose: / “For what purpose, O best of the gods, have we been remembered by you?”
Śakra said: / “Let the venerable ones hear the purpose: / on the Himācala, the daughter of the mountain is performing severe austerities.
In accordance with her cherished desire, you ought to bring about / the completion of the goddess’s austerities, with all haste, for the welfare of the world.”
Saying “So be it”, the sages went to that mountain frequented by hosts of Siddhas, / and then addressed her in gentle words:
“O daughter, lotus-eyed one, what wish of yours is resolved upon?” / Then the goddess, with respect and deference, spoke to the sages:
The goddess said: / “O illustrious ones, abandoning the silence of those practicing austerities like yourselves, / my mind, directed toward offering salutation, asks without hesitation.
With serene countenances, please first accept seats; / once seated and relieved of fatigue, you may then question me.”
Thus spoken to, they then took their seats there; / and she, having first worshipped them duly according to ritual,
spoke slowly to the seven sages, the munis who resembled the sun, / relinquishing her vow of silence and bowing duly to the sages.
When her silence had ended, the venerable Seven Sages as well / questioned her again, who had become the object of their respect.
She too, having a mind filled with reverence, smiling charmingly, / looked at all the sages, put aside her restraint of speech, and spoke:
"Venerable ones, you know what is desired in the hearts of living beings; / for embodied souls are exceedingly afflicted by the body and other [pains].
Some, however, being skillful, strive there through various endeavors; / unwearied, they indeed attain rare states by means of proper measures.
Others, having determined manifold undertakings, / undertake an energetic vow beneficial for attaining another body.
As for me, my hand stretches out again and again desiring to touch / the peak of the Vindhya, adorned with a garland of flowers born in the sky.
Indeed, I am striving to obtain God Bhava as my husband, / who is by nature hard to propitiate and is currently engaged in austerities,
whose nature is not comprehended by gods or demons, who is the refuge of ultimate reality and action; / and now, moreover, love has been burned by that one free from passion.
How can one like me propitiate such a lord, Śiva?" / Addressed thus, those sages, then wishing to know the firmness of her mind,
spoke words appropriate to the context, relating to the matter at hand. / The sages said: "O daughter, happiness in this world is conceived of as twofold:
the union of this body, and the delight of the mind. / But by his very nature he is space-clad, terrible, adorned with ashes and bones,
bearer of a skull, a naked beggar, deformed-eyed, inconsistent in actions, / frenzied, of an insane appearance, loathsome, and keeping such company.
There is no purpose to be sought with such an embodied misfortune as a husband, / if you desire everlasting happiness for your own body.
Then how can you [seek it] from Mahādeva, who consorts with goblins, who is disgusting, / whose ornaments are made of human marrow, driveling fat, bones, and skulls,
who is decorated with ornaments made of hissing, fierce serpent-kings, / who dwells in cremation grounds, and who is followed by terrible Pramathas?
There is Hari, whose feet are rubbed by the multitude of crowns of the lords of gods, slayer of enemies, / supporter of the world, beloved of Śrī, possessing infinite forms.
Likewise there is Indra, who enjoys sacrifices, praised in prayers, the punisher of Pāka; / and there is Fire, the treasury of the gods, granting all wishes.
There is the Wind, supporter of the world, who is the breath of all embodied beings; / and likewise King Vaiśravaṇa, the lord endowed with the glory of all wealth.
Why do you not desire to obtain one of these? / Or is the happiness desired by your mind to be obtained from another in this world?
This is so, O daughter: such is the power of worldly fortunes / for your attainment of welfare in this body or the next.
All that is offered to the gods already belongs to your father. / To obtain a groom, there is distress; and even he here is a fruitless tree.
For an object prayed for is generally competent and exceedingly rare; / because of being appointed to its proper station, O daughter, it is obtained even there."
Having spoken thus, the mountain's daughter, greatly angered at the best of sages, / spoke with eyes red with rage and twitching lips:
The goddess said: "What principle can there be in obstinacy? Where is there restraint in vice? / By whom can those who understand things contrarily be set upon the right path?
In this way you consider me to be of poor intellect, fond of misguided obstinacy in the wrong place. / There is no consideration for me, as if I were one proud with egoism.
You are all equal to Prajāpati, all-seeing; / do you truly not know that eternal God, the lord of the universe,
unborn, the sovereign ruler, unmanifest, of immeasurable rising majesty? / Let alone the reality of his deeds; his true awareness is veiled.
Even the lords of the gods, headed by Hari and Brahmā, do not know him. / As for his innate majesty manifested throughout the worlds,
conspicuous to all beings, do you even not know that? / Whose form is this sky? Whose is the fire? Whose is the wind?
Whose is the earth? Whose is Varuṇa? Who has the moon and the sun as eyes? / Whose linga do the gods and demons worship with devotion in all the worlds?
And do you not even know the power or the origin / of those gods headed by Brahmā, Īśvara, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the great sages?
The gods headed by Nārāyaṇa were born to Kaśyapa from Aditi; / Kaśyapa is the son of Marīci, and Aditi is the daughter of Dakṣa.
Both Marīci and Dakṣa are indeed the two sons of Brahmā; / Brahmā attained the fullness of his divine powers from the golden egg.
From whose meditation did he, being elemental and a part of the material world, become manifest? / Then indeed, by Nārāyaṇa himself, by taking resort in his own desire,
impelled by Him, he entered into this birth consisting of Nārāyaṇa. / That impulsion is said to be caused by karma alone for those who are helpless.
Just as the mind of one afflicted with insanity or the like becomes distorted, / he regards even agreeable objects as their opposites;
he always laughs at observed worldly affairs. / In the attainment of the fruits of dharma and adharma, understand [it to be] Viṣṇu.
O sages, sow these words of mine repeatedly in the proximity of Girīśa's ears, / just as farmers cast handfuls of good seed into an excellent field on the earth for an abundant yield."
Hearing her beneficial, lovely words that were appropriate to the procedure, / they, resembling the lord of speech, spoke, charming with smiles.
The sages said: "When the creation of the world has taken place, that highest duty is indeed true. / The doubt usually belongs to the Snowy Mountain at that time.
Truly, all those who are intent upon their mission are anxious; / the minds of those great souls hasten, but indeed,
the course of the world must be followed, especially by those who wish to speak [authoritatively], / because through that, dharma flourishes, and others hold to that authority."
Having said this, the sages went swiftly to the snow-mountain; / there they were respectfully received and honoured by that snow-mountain.
Pleased, yet in haste, the best of sages spoke briefly. / The sages said: "The god who wields the Pināka in person seeks your daughter.
Therefore, quickly purify yourself, as an oblation cast into the fire; / for that task of the gods has been revolving for a very long time.
This effort must be made for the deliverance of the universe." / Addressed thus at that time, the Mountain, overcome by a surge of joy,
became unable to speak an answer to the sages, as if making an entreaty. / Then Menā, having saluted the sages, agitated by affection,
herself spoke meaningful words to those sages regarding her daughter. / Menā said: "That great fruit for the sake of which people desire the birth of a daughter,
all of that has now presented itself in due course. / Even if a bridegroom is endowed with noble birth, youthful age, beauty, and sovereignty,
a daughter should not be summoned and given to him unasked. / He is space-clad, matted-haired, trident-bearing, and though he burned love, he is the granter of desires;
how indeed can that terrible one be worshipped by my daughter?" / The sages said: "Recognize the divine power of Śaṃkara, at the pair of whose lotus-like feet
gods and demons offer worship and find great peace. / Whatever form is suitable to someone, that is sought after for long by him.
The maiden performs terrible austerities, finding peace through that form; / since she will bring these divine vows to a conclusion,
she will certainly remain attentive toward us in this matter." / Having spoken thus, they went together with the Mountain to where the Mountain-born was.
Umā, who surpassed the heat of the sun and the flame of fire, consisting of the brilliance of tapas, / was addressed gently by the sages, and the proud maiden spoke meaningful words.
"Indeed I desire no mean [husband], but only Śarva, the wielder of the Pināka, / standing in supremacy, the bestower of supreme prosperity upon living beings."
His steadfastness, lordly acts, and authority are unequaled and great; / than whom there is nothing else higher, and from whom everything proceeds.
I have taken refuge in Him whose lordship is beginningless. / He is equanimous, active, yet in the long run the reverse [of worldly striving]."
Hearing these words of the goddess, the excellent sages then, / their eyes filled with tears of joy, embraced that ascetic maiden.
Extremely delighted, they spoke sweet words to the daughter of the mountain. / The sages said: / "Most wondrous, ah, daughter! You are like pure Knowledge embodied!"
You bring clarity to our thoughts because your refuge is devotion to Bhava. / Truly, we know the wondrous lordship of that god.
We came here only to test the firmness of your resolve. / Before long, O slender-limbed lady, this wish of yours will come to pass.
The sun departs with its radiance; what luster is separate from jewels? / What meaning remains if one abandons one's own colors? Likewise you without Giriśa.
We shall go to supplicate him by many expedients. / Moreover, this very objective rests deeply in our own hearts.
Therefore, you are indeed that wisdom, for you are policy itself; / hence Śaṅkara too will accomplish the purpose without doubt."
Having said this, all the sages, worshipped by the mountain's maiden, / set out to see Giriśa upon the great peak of Himavat.
Their bodies bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, their matted locks tied reddish-brown, / carrying garlands of mandāra flowers in their hands followed by bees,
having reached the mountain plateau, they beheld Śaṅkara's hermitage, / where the multitude of all creatures was tranquil, and the forest was hushed on all sides,

and the waters flowed silently without agitation in all directions. / There at the door they saw Vīraka holding a cane in his hand.

Those venerable sages, humble on account of the importance of the business, / the best of eloquent speakers, spoke to him in sweet words:
"Know that we have arrived here to see Śaṅkara, the lord of virtues, / the three-eyed one, impelled by a mission for the gods.
You alone are our recourse there, so that there may be no delay in time. / O master, such an entreaty is usually addressed to a doorkeeper."
Thus addressed by the sages, he then spoke to them with respect: / "He has gone to the Mandākinī to perform the twilight rite of the ritual."
In a moment, O twice-born ones, you will see the bearer of the trident." / Thus addressed, the sages, skilled in their affair, waited with care,
like cātaka birds in the rainy season longing for a deep raincloud. / Then, in a moment, when his customary ritual performance was complete,
seated in the vīrāsana posture, restrained upon a deer skin, / then Vīraka, humbly resting his knees upon the earth, gladly
spoke to the god, the sole refuge of love: / "The seven sages of radiant splendor have arrived to see you.

"O Lord, deign to command their seeing; therefore, [turn from] meditation here."
Having been addressed thus by that great-souled Vīraka, Dhūrjaṭi,

then gave permission for their entrance with a sign of a knit brow.
With a nod of his head, Vīraka too summoned those seven great sages,

who stood not far away, to behold Pinākin.
With their matted hair bound up in haste, clad in their own dangling black-antelope skins,

they then entered the divine altar-terrace of Girīśa, the lord.
With folded hands casting showers of heavenly flowers,

and having bowed to the pair of feet of Pinākin, O dwellers of heaven,
those sages were then looked upon tenderly by the trident-bearing god.
Then, having seen Girīśa, they together praised [him] joyfully:

The sages said:
"Ah, truly our purpose is fulfilled today! We behold your sprout-like feet, praised by the lords of gods.
By your abundant weight of virtues, please assign us the task: the protection of all."

Then, smiling, the omniscient one addressed the foremost of sages:
"Whatever purpose is in your heart, carry that out now."

Thus spoken to, the sages quickly went where the mountain's daughter was; / those who know distinctions spoke to Girijā in the mountain cave: / "Do not burn with ascetic heat this delightful form, beloved and captivating!"

"Śaṃkara is pleased with you; he will take your hand in marriage.
We, having been petitioned, came previously to your father.

Go home with your father; we are going to our own dwelling."
Thus addressed, thinking, "There truly is a fruit to my asceticism,"

she went in haste to the divine, beautifully adorned dwelling of her father.
Remaining there, that virtuous lady deemed that night to be equal to ten thousand years,

longing having arisen in the daughter of the snow-mountain to see Hara.
Then, at the auspicious hour sacred to Brahmā, friends performed her auspicious rites,

multitudes of various auspicious ceremonies in proper order according to rule,
with combinations of divine blessings in the highly auspicious palace.
The embodied seasons, granting every wish, waited upon the mountain; / and winds providing pleasure engaged in the work of sweeping the mountain clean.
In the mansions Śrī herself, the goddess, adorned with various decorations, [dwelled]; / splendour was in all things, and prosperity full of ornaments.

Gems, such as the wish-yielding jewel, and creepers as well as
great trees like the wish-granting trees attended upon the mountain on every side.

The embodied medicinal herbs, joined with divine herbs,
and saps, and minerals were all servants of the mountain.

Servants of that mountain, and all residents of the hermitage were busy;
all the rivers and oceans, whatever was immobile and mobile,

they all increased the glory of the snow-mountain.
Sages, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras were present.

The gods too, on Mount Gandhamādana, for Śaṃkara,
with materials for adornment prepared, stood in their pure forms.

Then the Grandfather, his eyes expanded large with love,
bound the crescent moon upon the matted locks of Śarva.

Fastening an extensive garland of skulls upon his head, Cāmuṇḍā
addressed Girīśa: "O Śaṃkara, beget a son,

who, having slain the family of the lord of the Daityas, will gratify me with blood."
Śauri, taking an ear-ornament jewel, a radiant necklace,

and a serpent ornament, stood ready before Śambhu.
Śakra, his expanded lotus face sweating with haste, held

his elephant-skin whose tip-foliage was smeared with fat.
The sharp winds blew, having the sharp luster of the snow-mountain.

They adorned the bull, the swift vehicle of Hara as fast as thought.
The sun, fire, and moon, abiding at the edge of Śambhu's eyes, shone forth,

giving their own splendor to the lord of the world, the witness of the deeds of the world.
He placed funeral-pyre ash having the luster of silver in the skull-bowl,

and bound with his hand a garland made of human bones.
The lord of spirits stood at a distance, filled with fear, before him.

Setting aside an ornament of great gems of various kinds brought by the giver of wealth,
with his own hand, with a bracelet of a shining lord of serpents,

the Lord himself made spotless Takṣaka his ear-ornament.
When the ornament was completed, the Lord was adorned with decorations.

There too they indeed became busy in person according to rule.
The delightful, rich, and auspicious herbs released all fresh juices.

Goddess Earth was busy, charming in every aspect of her being.
Varuṇa himself, taking ornaments rich in gems

and extraordinary flowers made of diverse jewels, [approached].
The omniscient god of all embodied beings stood adorned with those ornaments.

Fire too, having purified himself, was present with divine gold ornaments,
pure gold of natural form.

And the wind, pleasant to the touch, blew fragrance towards the lord.
Śatakratu, joyful and glorious, adorned with vajra-bracelets on his arms,

held the parasol, dazzling like the moon's rays, smiling.
The chiefs of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.

Playing very sweet music, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang.
In an instant the seasons sang and danced there.

And the swift attendants stood around, shaking the snowy mountain.
In due order the Creator, maker of the universe, slayer of the eyes of Bhaga, took his seat,

and performed the marriage rite together with his wife as prescribed.
Given water for respect by the king of mountains, entertained by the hosts of gods,

the destroyer of the city dwelt for that night there together with his wife.
Then, awakened by the song of the Gandharvas, by the dance of the Apsarases,

and by the praises of the gods and Daityas, the lord of the gods,
having bidden farewell to the lord of the snow-mountain, at dawn, together with his wife,

went to Mount Mandara on the horned [bull] having the speed of the wind.
Then, when the lord Nīlalohita had departed with Umā, having enjoyed pleasure, the mountain,

accompanied by his relatives—whose mind indeed in the world, being a daughter's father, does not become free of restraints?—
In delightful city gardens and in secluded forests,

with heart deeply enamored, the destroyer of the eye of Bhaga dallied with the goddess.
Then, after much time, the mountain's daughter, playing the role of a mother,

played along with her companions with artificial little sons.
Once, the mountain-born goddess, having anointed her body with fragrant oil,

rubbed down her body, covered with dirt, with cleansing pastes.
Taking that cleansing paste, she made a man with the face of an elephant.

The playing goddess tossed that human figure into the water
of the auspicious Jāhnavī, her friend; thereupon he became one of vast body.

With an extremely huge body, he then filled the universe.
"Son!" the goddess said to him, and "Son!" said Jāhnavī.

The elephant-faced one was worshipped by the gods as Gāṅgeya,
and the Grandfather granted him the overlordship of the Vināyakas.

Again, that fair-complexioned lady, playing, made a tree,
with lovely sprouts grown from an aśoka tree, that fair-faced lady.

And she nurtured it, having auspicious sacramental rites performed
by Brahmins led by Bṛhaspati, the family priest of the lord of heaven.

Then the goddess was addressed with these words by the gods together with the sages:
"Now that a path has been shown, you ought to establish a limit.

What fruit will there be, O goddess, from little tree-sons nurtured?"
Having been spoken to thus, her limbs filled with joy, she spoke very auspicious words:

"The wise person who causes one well to be made in a waterless village
shall dwell in heaven for a year for every drop of water.
A stepwell is equal to ten wells; a reservoir is equal to ten stepwells; / a daughter is equal to ten reservoirs; and a tree is equal to ten daughters.
This indeed is the auspicious, ordained standard for the welfare of the world." / Being praised thus, the brāhmaṇas headed by Bṛhaspati
went to their own dwellings, having bowed to Bhavānī, the mother. / When they had gone, the god Śaṅkara, holding the hand
of the mountain's daughter, went to his own abode, / which brought delight to the mind, adorned with mansions, watchtowers, and gates,
with hanging pearl garlands, platforms crowded with flower-wreaths, / richly embellished with gold—a pleasure-house delightful to the heart,
filled with the fragrance of scattered flowers, echoing with the humming of intoxicated bees, / with its interior walls echoing with the songs sung by Kinnaras,
pervaded by clouds of fragrant incense, an unimaginable realm attainable only by thought, / supplied all around with eager domestic peahens for play,
with crystal archways where flocks of swans congregated, / clear, undisturbed, and crowded with Kinnaras in great numbers,
where the ruby-inlaid walls, reflecting pearls, / are stared at by parrots mistaking them for pomegranate seeds.
There the god began to play at dice with his beloved, / where the two remained sporting upon a surface of pure sapphire.
they attained bodily union, completely absorbed in the pleasure of diversion. / As the goddess and Śaṅkara were thus amusing themselves there,
a great sound arose, pervading the expanse of the sky. / Hearing it, out of curiosity, the goddess, amazed,
asked Hara, the best of the gods, "What is this?" / The god said, "This has never been seen by you before, O lady of sweet smiles.
These are the gaṇeśas, forever dear to me, sporting upon this mountain. / By austerity, celibacy, chanting my names, and visiting sacred shrines,
those best among men by whom I was pleased in the past / have reached my presence; they are dear to my heart, O fair-faced lady.
Taking any form at will, full of great zeal, endowed with noble forms and virtues, / I am filled with wonder at the deeds of these mighty ones.
They are capable of creating and destroying this world along with the gods. / Even if abandoned by Brahmā, the Moon, Indra, and the Gandharvas, together with Kinnaras and great serpents,
I am never bereft of them, nor do I ever take delight without them. / They are dear to my heart, O lady of lovely limbs, and they are sporting upon the mountain."
Thus spoken to, the goddess then, leaving him, confounded by astonishment, / reached the aperture of a window and looked out with a startled face.
All those who were there—some lean, tall, short, stout, and pot-bellied, / some with faces like tigers and elephants, some in the forms of sheep and goats,
having forms of various creatures, with fiery mouths, dark and reddish-brown, / gentle, terrible, smiling-faced, always with black and reddish matted locks,
with faces like diverse birds, with diverse divine faces, / wearing silk and animal hides, naked, and others deformed,
cow-eared, elephant-eared, with many mouths, eyes, and bellies, / many-footed, many-armed, carrying various divine weapons in their hands,
crowned with wreaths of diverse flowers, various, wild, and fearsome, / bearing various weapons, adorned with various armor,
mounted upon wondrous vehicles, having divine forms, roving through the sky, / resounding with the playing of vīṇās and other musical instruments, dancing in various stances.
Seeing those gaṇeśas of such nature, the goddess said to Śaṅkara: / The goddess said: / "How many are these gaṇeśas counted to be? What are their names, and what is their nature?
Tell me of them one by one, those who are stationed individually." / Śaṅkara said: / "They are counted in hundreds of millions, renowned for their various deeds of valor.
The entire world is filled with these terrible beings of great strength. / In holy shrines, on highways, in ruined gardens, in houses,
in the bodies of Dānavas, in children, and in madmen / they enter joyfully, sustaining themselves on diverse foods and sports.
Some drink vapor, some drink foam, some drink smoke, some drink honey; / some eat fat, some drink blood, some eat everything, and some take no food at all.

Some eat what is offered to gods, some take the food of ascetics, and some take pleasure in diverse musical instruments. / Because of their endlessness, these gaṇas cannot indeed be described individually."
The goddess said: / "Wearing an elephant's hide as an upper garment, with clean limbs, wearing a muñja grass girdle, / his face painted restlessly with the paste of realgar,
wearing a charming garland of blue lotuses bitten by bees, / keeping time upon a raised bell-metal cymbal with a piece of stone,
what is the name of this gaṇa leader, O god, who is followed by Kinnaras, / who repeatedly turns his ear to the songs of the gaṇas?"

Śarva said:
"This is Vīraka, O goddess, ever dear to my heart, / an abode of manifold wonderful virtues, worshiped by the hosts of the lords of the Gaṇas."

The goddess said:
"I have a longing for such a son, O destroyer of the cities! / When shall I see such a son who brings delight?"

Śarva said:
"Let this very one be your son, bringing joy to your eyes. / For with you as his mother, Vīraka too has attained his purpose, O slender-waisted lady!"
Having said this, the daughter of the mountain king sent her friend Vijayā, / who was eager to gladden [her], to bring Vīraka at once.
She descended in haste from the sky-touching palace / toward the leader of the Gaṇas standing amidst the host, radiant as ten million suns.

Vijayā said:
"Come, Vīraka! By your playful charm the goddess has been pleased; / she calls you." Addressed thus, he dropped the piece of stone,
and approached the goddess, slowly followed by Vijayā, / his splendor resembling an open red lotus on the palace peak.
Seeing him, her breasts oozed with abundant sweet milk. / Girijā said: "Drink this flowing milk, my child; drink as much as you wish!"
The goddess spoke lovingly with words of sweet syllables: / "Come, my little son! You are born to me this very day, given to me now by the God of gods, O Vīraka!"
Having spoken, the mountain's daughter took him upon her lap, embraced him, and kissed his cheek. / Smelling his head and stroking his limbs, she adorned him herself with celestial ornaments,
with jingling bells, girdles, anklets, armlets strung with fine jewels, priceless pearl-strings, / soft blossoms, auspicious painted patterns, and charming bangles born of divine mantras.

Then, with abundant pure white mustard seeds mixed together, she performed the rite of limb-protection for him; / taking him up thus and placing a garland upon his head bright with decorative lines of yellow pigment, she spoke:

"Dear child, play now with the Gaṇas; remain vigilant, and move about slowly, avoiding chasms. / The trees on the mountain slopes are swarming with serpents, their branches broken by rutting elephants, exceedingly fragile.

Do not enter the forest frequented by numerous tigers, agitated by the turbulent waters of the Gaṅgā's realm. / In these manifold difficult terrains, O child, may one with a pure heart behold Vīraka's nature as my son!

May every good that is prayed for come to pass! Let whatever is to happen be auspicious." Having thus completed all the rites, / Vīraka, spoken to in this way by her, his mind captivated by playfulness, smiled and said to his mother:
"This bracelet was made for me by my mother herself, decorated with markings of pale-red dots, / and this tender garland made of lovely mālatī flowers was placed upon my head.
I shall please the Sovereign Lady!" Thinking thus, Vīraka went outside in haste to play / accompanied by his own Gaṇas, delighted, moving from south to west, and from west to north.

Coming from the north to the east accompanied by her friend, the daughter of the mountain watched from the window / that boy Vīraka playing outside, longing for a son out of worldly affection, since he was born of her womb.

Who, having little knowledge and dull-witted, bearing a body composed of flesh, feces, and urine, could succumb to delusion / so as to peer into the inner apartments, when the lords dwelling in heaven and the moon-crested god had entered the chambers?

Mounting their vehicles in this manner, the guardians of the directions then said to the throng of attendants for a moment: / 'This sword has become swordless, clean and sharp; whose sword has been taken by whom? Tell us!

Let it not be by the staff in hand! What shall we say? There is no business on the mountain with a fierce-formed courtyard. / This noose is here; who can be bound by it here? Do not stand about in vain, attendants of the guardians of the world!'

Saying, 'It is just so,' having seen the attendant of the god, the guardian Vīraka, / the goddess said to the protectors of the spirits in the forest, on the mountain, and on the ground at the entrance to the hall of the immortal sacrificial fire:

'Do not plunge into the falling waters of the torrents, nor into the dwellings covered with meshes of flowers, / nor into the hollows of diverse high mountain groves, nor willingly venture to resist the blasts of wind.

On the ground where gold-summited peaks descend, endowed with a yellowish luster from contact with heaps of golden dust, / and in the delightful forest of the sky-wanderers, the abundance of beauty of the host shone forth to dwell.

In the caves of Mandara, on the banks of delightful ponds, amidst kunda and mandāra flowers, sprouts, and lotuses, / the nectar of his form was drunk in by the women of the Siddhas with wide-open, unblinking eyes.'

Within a moment, the daughter of the mountain remembered Vīraka, eager for a son and desirous of amusement; / he too, having attained a rise of merit in that very moment, became her son in another birth on that account.

How could satisfaction arise for him as he played, who was fashioned by the creator of the universe by his splendor? / For a moment watching, for a moment listening to divine song, for a moment bustling about with the hosts eager to dance,

for a moment on a boulder bustling with the roar of lions, for a moment amidst large sāla and tāla trees blazing with clusters of gems, / for a moment amid the flowering rows of various tamāla trees, for a moment at the foot of a tree with restless swans,

for a moment in waters with little mud, seated on lotuses, for a moment in the auspicious, spotless lap of his mother; / sporting about, extending his childish play, the lord of the chiefs of Gaṇas bringing joy to the goddess.
In the bowers, accustomed to high songs by Vidyādharas, playful with amorous sports like the wielder of the Pināka, / having illuminated the world with his rays, when the sun had set,
the mountain standing afar in another land then followed behind, / as if making his firm friendship shine forth in his heart.
The glorious son of Vighanas, continually worshipped by the brāhmaṇas, / the mountain Meru, did not perform a favor for the sun about to fall.
Such is the order of things heard among men: indeed, when one slips downward, / the sun followed by the day, filling his own kin [with distress].
As long as the sages sat facing the sun with hands folded in twilight devotion, / so quickly was the day enveloped in heat warded off.
Then night's darkness gradually expanded in this world, / like pollution corrupting the mind in the heart of a crooked man.
In an inner chamber whose walls were illuminated by the gem-lamps of blazing serpent hoods, / upon a couch whose upper covering was of jeweled cloth resembling a host of moons,
vying with the rainbow through the glitter of various jewels, / adorned with radiant rows of pearls and nets of small jeweled bells,
under a sky covered by a lovely canopy swaying gracefully, / when Śiva together with the daughter of the mountain had entered with slow steps on Mount Mandara,
he stood with his neck embraced by the creeper-like arms of the daughter of the mountain, / his range of vision completely filled by the abundant moonlight blended with the moon.
The mountain-born goddess also, having dark corners of her eyes and the luster of blue lotus petals, / when joined with the night, became exceedingly dark.

Then the god spoke to her, who was endowed with the arts of playful dalliance.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, entitled 'Description of the Marriage of Gaurī,' in the first part, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.44.m: Śarva said: / 'O slender-limbed lady, on my white body you, of dark luster, shine / like a black female serpent clinging to a white sandalwood tree.
United with the moonlight and covered in blood-red garments, / like a dark night in the dark fortnight, you cause a defect to my sight.'
Thus spoken to by him, Girijā, shouting at the top of her voice, / spoke to the wielder of the Pināka with eyes red with anger and a face distorted by a frown:
The goddess said: / 'Every person is humiliated by dullness of their own making; / necessarily a petitioner incurs insult, O moon-bedecked god!
Since I sought you by means of long-practiced austerities, / for that reason indeed, this humiliation is met at every step.
I am neither crooked nor discordant, O Śarva, O Dhūrjaṭi! / You are known to the world as venomous, and a refuge for the moon, a manifest mine of flaws.
Indeed, you knock out teeth and are the slayer of Bhaga's eyes; / the divine sun, twelvefold in nature, knows you well.
You cause pain in my head, reviling me for your own faults; / you who call me "Kṛṣṇā" (dark lady) are celebrated as Mahākāla (great black one/death).
I shall go to the mountain to abandon my life through austerities; / what use have I for living, insulted by a rogue,
by a low Kāpālika who dwells constantly in the cremation ground, / his limbs smeared with ashes, roaming in the midst of the Mātṛs?'
Hearing her speech with words sharp with anger, Hara, / agitated by misfortune, spoke with his moon-crested head trembling.
Śarva said: / 'You are the daughter of the mountain, O Girijā; I am not intent on reproaching you. / Thinking it flattering speech, an occasion of infatuation was produced by me.
The doubt is in a sound mind; it was not my intention to offend, O Girijā. / If you are so angered, O timid one, then to you I shall certainly never again
speak in jest! Abandon your anger, O sweetly smiling lady! / This gesture of folded hands has been made to you by me with bowed head.
A low man indeed undergoes change through insult and reproach; / a man whose vital spots are touched might be of the wicked, but not of the virtuous.
Though appeased by the god with many flatteries, the goddess, / struck in her vital parts, being virtuous, did not abandon her fierce anger.
Then tearing away her garment that had been seized by Śaṅkara's hand, / her locks disheveled, the daughter of the mountain wished to depart in haste.
As she was departing in anger, the destroyer of the cities spoke again: / 'Truly, with all your limbs you show resemblance to your father!
The mind on the peak of the Himalayas is just tangled with nets [of trees]; / so also your disposition is deeper than unfordable depths.
Hardness [derived] from the stones, multiplicity of limbs from the forests, / crookedness from the rivers, and difficulty of approach from the snow—
all this has passed into you from the snowy mountain, O slender-limbed lady!' / Addressed thus, the mountain maiden spoke again to Giriśa,
her head trembling with anger, her lips quivering. / Umā said: 'All [such talk] would arise through the imputation of fault, by falsely censuring the virtuous.
Into you too everything has passed from contact with the wicked: / multiplicity of tongues from serpents, an unloving nature from ashes,
