pollution of the heart derived from the moon, and intolerance even from poison. / Furthermore, what is the use of speaking much here? Enough of the weariness of your words!
From living in the cremation ground you are fearless; from being naked you have no shame; / from being a bearer of a skull you are merciless; your compassion departed long ago.'
Having spoken thus, the mountain-born goddess went out from that temple; / as that goddess of gods was going, shouts of joy were made by the Gaṇas.
"Where are you going, mother?" they cried, running after her in tears. / Clasping both feet of the goddess, Vīraka, his voice choked with tears,
said: "Mother, what is this? Where are you going, agitated with anger? / I will follow you as you depart, stripped of affection.
Otherwise, abandoned by you, I shall throw myself down from the summit of this mountain!" / Raising his face with her right hand,
the mother said to Vīraka: "Do not grieve, my son! / It is not right for you to jump from the mountain peak, nor to go with me.
Hear the purpose for which I am going, my son: / having been called 'Black' by Hara, I have been stunned and humiliated.
Therefore, I shall perform austerities by which I may attain the state of Gaurī. / This god is fond of women; when I have departed,
you must guard the door and constantly watch for vulnerabilities, / so that no other woman enters there into Hara's presence.
If you see another woman, inform me, my son; / I shall quickly do whatever is proper thereafter."
"Let it be so!" Vīraka then said to the queen of gods, / his body bathed by the nectar of his mother's command, his distress removed.
Having bowed down to his mother, he went to oversee the guard. / And the goddess saw approaching an adorned friend of her mother,
named Kusumamohinī, the goddess of that mountain. / She too, seeing the mountain's daughter, her mind distraught with affection,
embraced her and said aloud: "Where are you going, my daughter?" / She related everything to her—the cause of her anger toward Śaṃkara.
Then Girijā spoke again to that goddess who was like a mother to her. / Umā said: "O blameless one, you are the eternal goddess of this supreme king of mountains;
your presence is everywhere, and you are exceedingly affectionate in heart. / Therefore I shall tell you what must be done by you, O motherly one:
The entrance of any other woman must be zealously guarded against by you; / he should constantly be served with great care in secret upon this mountain.
If any woman enters the presence of the Pināka-wielder, you must tell me, O faultless one; / then I shall do whatever is appropriate thereafter."
Having been spoken to thus and having said 'So be it,' the auspicious goddess went to the mountain; / Umā, the daughter of the mountain, also went to her father's wonderful garden.
Reaching the open expanse, dark as a bank of clouds, / she took off her ornaments, wore tree-bark garments,
and stood there: in summer heated by the five fires, in the rainy season dwelling in water, / subsisting on wild foods or fasting, sleeping on the bare ground.
While she remained there practicing austerities in this manner, / in the meantime a mighty Daitya, learning that the mountain's daughter had gone,
a son of Andhaka, rejoiced, recalling the slaying of his father; / having conquered all the gods in battle, this brother of Baka, fierce in combat,
named Āḍi, ever seeking an opportune opening against the moon-crested god, / that enemy of the gods came to the city of the slayer of Tripura.
Arriving there, he saw Vīraka standing at the doorway; / and he remembered the boon that had been granted to him by the Lotus-born [Brahmā].
When the Daitya Andhaka was slain by Giriśa, the enemy of the Asuras, / Āḍi had performed vast and extremely severe austerities.
Brahmā, pleased by his austerities, approached and said: / "What do you wish to obtain through your austerities, O best of Dānavas?"
The Daitya said to Brahmā: "I choose freedom from death." / Brahmā said: "For those born in this world of transmigration, there is no escape from death;
by one means or another, O lord of Daityas, death must come to embodied beings." / Spoken to thus, that lion among Daityas said to the Lotus-born:
"When a change of my form takes place, O Lotus-born, / then let my death occur; otherwise, let me be immortal!"
Having been spoken to thus, the lotus-born [Brahmā], pleased, then said: / 'When the second transformation of your form will take place,
"then your death shall occur; otherwise it shall not happen." / Spoken to thus, that mighty son of the Daitya considered himself immortal.
At that time, recalling the means for his own death, / he did not come within the range of the sight of Vīraka, the guardian.
Taking the form of a serpent, entering through an aperture, / that terrible, invincible Dānava avoided the line of sight of the lord of the Gaṇas.
Unperceived by the lord of the Gaṇas, having entered, / that great Asura then cast off his serpent form and assumed another body.

In order to delight Giriśa, that fool
assumed an illusory form of Umā, unthinkable and enchanting,

complete with all limbs, endowed with all her distinguishing marks;
and within the vulva, the Daitya placed a firm tooth made of diamond.

With sharp tip, intent on killing Giriśa through confusion of intellect,
the Daitya, having fashioned the appearance of Umā's form, approached Hara.

Sinful, yet of lovely appearance, arrayed in wondrous ornaments and garments—
seeing him, Giriśa was pleased, and embracing that great Asura,

taking him to be the mountain's daughter in all intermediate limbs,
he asked, “O mountain's daughter, is your good disposition not feigned,

you who, knowing my heart, have arrived here, O fair-complexioned one?
Bereft of you, my abode, the three worlds, was empty.

You have arrived, O one of serene face; such conduct is indeed fitting for you.”
Thus addressed, the lord of the Dānavas smiled softly and spoke to him.

there I found no pleasure; therefore I have returned to your presence.”
Thus addressed, Śaṃkara felt doubt in his mind, and reflecting,

steadying himself in his heart, the god, with a smiling face,
knowing she was not angry, yet firm in her vow by nature,

thought: “Has she returned without attaining her desire? What is this, knowingly?”
Reflecting thus, Hara scrutinized her distinguishing marks.

He did not see on her left side that mark characterized by a lotus,
formed by a whorl of hair; thereupon the god who holds the Pināka,

perceiving that Dānava illusion, and concealing his inner purpose,
took up the weapon with a phallic tusk and struck down that Dānava.

Vīraka, the gatekeeper, did not comprehend that event,
having seen the lord of the Dānavas in female form, fragrant with flowers.

The daughter of the snow mountain was quickly informed by the messenger, the Wind.
Having heard from the mouth of the Wind, the goddess's eyes turned red with anger.

She looked upon her son Vīraka, her heart burning with pain.
The goddess said:
“Since, abandoning me, your mother, agitated by affection,

you granted women opportunity in secret with Śaṃkara,
therefore among mortals you shall have a harsh, dull, and heartless mother

resembling the form of Gaṇeśa, a rock for a mother.
This cause is well known out of love for the son Vīraka,

in origin and procedure, a doubt resolved by a wondrous narrative.”
Immediately after the curse had thus been cast by the mountain's daughter,

from her mouth came forth anger in the form of a mighty lion.
That lion had a terrifying face, with its neck bristling with manes,

its tail raised upward, its gaping jaw formidable with fangs,
its mouth wide open, its tongue dangling, slender in belly and other limbs of strength.

The goddess stood ready then to abide in his mouth.
Knowing what was in her mind, the four-faced lord

came to that hermitage, which was the abode of all fortunes.
Arriving, the lord of gods spoke to the mountain-born goddess with clear words.

Brahmā said:
“What more do you desire to obtain? What unobtainable thing shall I give you?
Desist from this extremely painful penance at my command!”

Hearing that, the mountain-born goddess, constrained by deference to the teacher,
spoke words wishing to discard the dark complexion uttered by Hara’s voice.

Therefore may I become golden-hued, endowed with that name,
so that half the body of the husband, the lord of spirits, may become venom-free.”

Hearing those words of hers, the lord of the universe said:
“So be it! And again you shall share half your husband's body!”

Then she cast off that black sheath resembling a blooming blue lotus;
and that sheath became a formidable goddess, bell in hand, three-eyed,

adorned with all kinds of ornaments, wearing yellow silk.
Then Brahmā spoke to that goddess who had the luster of a blue lotus:

“O Niśā, from contact with the body of the mountain-born goddess, at my command
you have attained fulfillment of purpose; you shall advance as Ekānaṃśā.

This lion that arose from the goddess's anger, O fair-faced one,
let it be your mount, O goddess, and let it be on your banner, being of great strength.

Go to the Vindhya mountain; there you will perform the work of the gods.
This Yakṣa named Pañcāla, who is followed by a hundred thousand Yakṣas,

is given by me as your attendant, O goddess, endowed with hundreds of illusions.”
Having thus spoken, the goddess Kauśikī went to the Vindhya mountain.

Umā too, having accomplished her desire, went into the presence of Giriśa.
As she was entering, Vīraka, attentive,

stopped the goddess from the doorway, holding a golden cane rod;
and in anger he spoke to her, whose appearance had deviated [from the dark]:

“You have no business here; go away before you are devoured!
A Daitya wearing the form of the goddess came to deceive the god;

he entered, but he was not seen [by me], and he was killed by the god.
And once he was killed, I was commanded by the angered blue-throated one:

‘Since I observe this inattention of yours at the door,
you shall not be my doorkeeper for many groups of years!’

Therefore I will not grant you entrance here; depart at once!
Except for the one mountain's daughter, the mother tender with affection,

no other woman obtains entrance, O lotus-eyed one!”
When he had spoken thus, the goddess then reflected in her mind:

“That was not a woman at all, but a son of Diti, of whom the Wind told me;
in vain was Vīraka cursed by me, overcome by anger!

Improper deeds are often done by fools possessed by wrath;
by anger fame is destroyed, anger kills established prosperity.

Without discerning the true facts, I cursed my son!
To those whose minds perceive things wrongly, the arrival of misfortune is easy.”

Having reflected thus, the mountain-born goddess spoke this to Vīraka,
with her lotus-bright face showing the signs of rising shame:

The goddess said:
“O Vīraka, I am your mother; let there be no confusion in your mind.
I am the beloved of Śaṃkara, daughter of the snow-peaked mountain.

Do not entertain doubt, my son, due to the delusion of my bodily hue;
this fair complexion was given to me by the pleased lotus-born one.

You were cursed by me because the event devised by the Daitya was known [to me],
knowing that a woman had entered while Śaṃkara stayed in secret.

The curse cannot be revoked; nevertheless, I say to you:
you will soon return from the human state, endowed with all desires.”

Saluting with his head his mother, his mind fulfilled,
he praised the chaste one, shining like the full moon, the daughter of the snow mountain:

Vīraka said:
“O you whose foot-nails flash with the luster of the best gems gleaming on the bowed crests of gods and Asuras,
O daughter of the mountain, affectionate to those who seek refuge, destroyer of the afflictions of bowed beings as they bow again and again!

O you whose neck is adorned with the circle of the sun, who steal away the brilliance of the vast golden mountain,
terrified by the clinging of adverse misfortunes, O mountain's daughter, I take refuge in you!

Who else in the world has instantly bestowed upon those bowed the object of their desires, as you have done?
To whom in the world would the moon-crested one, the earth-supporter, and the sages bow, as they do to you?”

You were created through spotless yoga, unconquerable, having an assembly of mighty lords equal to your slender form; / crushing the hosts of Andhaka's kin, you were first praised by the foremost of the gods.

Your neck is lifted high with a mass of white manes; you stand upon the rushing speed of Bhava's great king of beasts; / your long multitude of arms crushed the great asuras, tawny as the fire from the mouth of your pure spear.

You are proclaimed by the worlds as Aticaṇḍikā, O Mother, slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha; / swift on earth, your sole delight is pacifying worldly afflictions and dānavas, granting whatever is wished by those bowed [before you].

Whatever body of yours is in the sky, in the path of the wind, in the fire-filled space, or upon the earth, O goddess, / to that unconquerable, peerless [form], O beloved of Bhava, conceiver of the worlds, I bow.

The oceans with charming, towering waves, the fire whose blazing burned all moving and unmoving things, / and the serpents bearing thousands of hoods—bestowing fearlessness, you shall tell me [of your grace].

O goddess, refuge of steadfastly devoted people, I have come to the shelter of your feet; / may all my faculties here be obedient to your command, granting the experience of the bliss of your playful grace.
Highly pleased when thus praised by Vīraka, / the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, entered the auspicious dwelling of her husband.
Vīraka, standing at the door, dismissed the gods who longed for a sight of Hara, / sending them back to their own homes with due respect.
"There is no opportunity here, O gods; Vṛṣākapi is playing / in secret with the goddess." Addressed thus, they departed as they had come.
When a thousand years had passed, the gods, eager in their minds, / dispatched the Fire to find out what Śaṅkara was doing.
Entering through a bird-crevice in the form of a parrot, the Fire-god / saw everything as [Śiva] lay on the couch making love with the daughter of the mountain.
And the lord of the gods saw him, the Fire-god in the form of a parrot. / Filled with some anger, Mahādeva spoke to him:
Śarva said: / "Half of my seed was cast into the goddess, O parrot-formed one, / and through bashfulness she ceased; drink the [other] half, O Pāvaka.
Since this hindrance was caused by you, it is fitting that it go into you." / Addressed thus, the Fire with folded hands drank the deposited seed.
Because of that, the gods became permeated [by it], since Fire is their mouth; / then, tearing open their bellies, that seed belonging to Maheśvara
came forth, shining like molten gold, in the extensive hermitage of Śaṅkara. / In that place there arose a vast, spotless lake many leagues wide,
with blooming golden lotuses, resonant with various birds. / Hearing of that lake and the great golden lotus that had arisen,
the goddess went, filled with curiosity, to that lake of golden lotuses. / Having sported in the water there, and having made a crest of that lotus,
the goddess then sat down on its bank, surrounded by her female companions. / Wishing to drink that water, sweet, pure, and filled with lotuses,
she saw those Kṛttikās, all six resembling the splendor of the sun, / who had taken that water in a lotus leaf and were setting out for home.
With delight she said: "I wish to drink the water resting in the lotus leaf." / Then all the Kṛttikās spoke to the daughter of the snowy mountain:
The Kṛttikās said: / "We will give it to you, beloved, on condition that the one who is born in your womb / shall also be our son, our protector, and provide our livelihood,
and be renowned in all the three worlds, O fair-faced one!" / Addressed thus, the daughter of the mountain said: "How can a son,
equipped with all the limbs born of my body, belong to you all?" / Then the Kṛttikās said to her: "We shall certainly fashion
noble heads and noble limbs for him, if it shall be so." / Spoken to thus, the daughter of the mountain said: "Let it be so, blameless ones!"
Then, filled with joy, they gave her the water resting in the lotus leaf, / and she gradually drank that water.
And when that water was drunk, in that very instant an excellent [child], / tearing open the goddess's right flank, emerged.
A wondrous boy came forth, destroyer of sickness and sorrow, / a powerful lord possessing a multitude of arrays of sunbeams,
bearing a spotless, aloft spear, trident, and goad, like a blazing fire; / having a golden complexion, he arose to slay the daityas.
For this reason indeed he became known as Kumāra. / Then another child came forth, tearing open the goddess's left flank,
Skanda; or rather, that six-faced slayer of foes came from the bright mouth of Fire, / purely from the water of the Kṛttikās, through branches (śākhās) especially.
Auspicious branches were said to be spread across his six faces; / because of that, this six-faced one was called Viśākha in the worlds.
He became famed as Skanda, Viśākha, the Six-Faced One (Ṣaḍvaktra), and Kārtikeya. / On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, the two mighty ones,
resembling the sun, were born in the vast reed forest. / And on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, these two, born of fire,
were made into one from the two boys at twilight for the sake of prosperity. / Then on that very sixth day, the lord Guha was consecrated
by all the hosts of immortals—Brahmā, Upendra, Indra, and the Sun— / with fragrances, auspicious garlands, incense, and also with playthings,
with umbrellas, masses of chowries, ornaments, and unguents; / the six-faced lord was duly consecrated according to rule.
Śakra gave him his daughter, famed as Devasenā, / to be his wife, and Viṣṇu, lord of the gods, then gave a weapon.
The lord of wealth gave him a million yakṣas; / the Fire gave his splendor, and the Wind gave a vehicle.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave a toy: a cock capable of assuming any form at will. / In this way, all those gods, their hearts joyful,
gave an endless retinue to Skanda, who possessed the splendor of the sun. / Falling on their knees upon the ground, the hosts of gods praised him,
the foremost among the gods praising the boon-granting six-faced one with this hymn: / The gods said: "Salutation to Kumāra of great radiance, and to Skanda who crushed the dānavas!
Salutation to you whose splendor is like the orb of the morning sun, to Guhya, to Guha! / Salutation to you, remover of the world's fear! Salutation to you, devoted to compassion for the world!
Salutation to the broad- and clean-eyed one! Salutation to Viśākha of great vows! / Homage, homage to you, furious in battle! Salutation to the one whose radiant mount is a peacock!
Salutation to you, wearer of armlets! Salutation to you, who hold an aloft banner! / Salutation to you, bowed to by majestic might! Salutation to the bearer of the bell, endowed with steadfastness!"
Kumāra said: / "What desire of yours shall I grant? Tell me without distress, / even if it is a task thought to be impossible, long pondered in your hearts."
Having been spoken to thus by him, the gods, bowing their heads, / all with delighted minds, spoke to the high-souled Guha:
"A king of daityas named Tāraka, the bringer of an end to the entire race of immortals, / is mighty, invincible, fierce, wicked in conduct, and exceedingly wrathful.
Slay that unassailable daitya who destroys everything! / A remaining duty has approached us, and it brings terror.
And fierce Hiraṇyakaśipu, unslayable by the hosts of gods, / is a destroyer of sacrifices and an evildoer, by whom even Brahmā was tormented.
Destroy these two! May good fortune be yours, and your great might!" / Thus addressed, saying "So be it," following the path of all the immortals,
The lord of the worlds set out, praised by the chiefs of the gods, / for the destruction of Tāraka, the thorn of the worlds.
Then Śakra, having secured a secret haven, sent / a messenger speaking harsh words to the lion among the Dānavas.
Having gone there, fearless, he spoke to the Daitya of terrifying appearance. / The messenger said: / "Śakra, the lord of the gods, the master of heaven, speaks to you, the banner of the Daityas:
O Tārakāsura, prepare yourself as you wish, with all your might. / For the sin you have committed, blazing like fire through the world,
I am its destroyer today; I am the king in the three worlds." / Hearing these astonishing words, his eyes reddened with rage,
the evil-minded one, whose glory was almost ruined, spoke to the messenger. / Tāraka said: / "O Śakra, your prowess has been seen hundreds of times in great battle.
Because of your shamelessness, you have no peace, O evil-minded Śakra!" / When this had been said and the messenger had departed, the Dānava reflected:
"Śakra would not be able to speak thus here without finding a haven. / From this support, it is understood that Skanda has now been born from Śakra."
Then he saw a host of evil omens foretelling destruction: / a shower of dust and a fall of blood from the sky upon the surface of the earth,
a trembling of his left eye, a mental parching of his mouth, / and he perceived a wilting of the lotus-faces of his own people.
And he saw fierce, evil creatures uttering ominous cries. / Without even reflecting upon that, the son of Diti became absorbed in mind at that moment,
when [he beheld] the army of the heaven-dwellers, terrible with the deep ringing sound of bells on troops of elephants, / likewise adorned with the neighing and eager spirits of hosts of horses,
resplendent with towering royal banners amidst the troops, / and with aerial chariots of wondrous forms having pure, waving chowries,
decked with ornaments, resounding with songs sung by Kinnaras, / wearing chaplets of blooming flowers from various heavenly trees,
bearing spotless shields that spread wide without sorrowful weapons, / holding a radiant gleam rich like lightning, resounded with various musical instruments—
standing on his palace, the Daitya beheld that army of the heaven-dwellers. / He then reflected, his mind somewhat bewildered:
"Who could be this unprecedented warrior whom I have not conquered?" / Then, troubled with anxiety, the Daitya heard harsh words, / this terrifying utterance proclaimed by Siddhas and bards:
"Victory, O most excellent Kumāra, whose staff-like arms are immensely fierce in the radiance of your peerless spear, / whose sportive eyes cause the lotus-faces of the impetuous gods to bloom!

Victory, O submarine fire to the great ocean of the lineage of Diti's sons, who have a charming peacock chariot, / O Mahāsena, the shoots of whose toenails are bent low by millions of crowns of the gods!
Victory, O you whose waving, lovely topknot is adorned with fresh, spotless lotuses, / an irresistible forest-fire to the lineage of the Daitya kings, charming in your staff!
Victory, O Lord Viśākha! Victory, O child who alleviates the sorrow of the hosts of worlds in seven days! / Victory, O Skanda, the destroyer of the leaders among Diti's sons across all the worlds!"
Hearing all this proclaimed by the divine bards, / Tāraka remembered the word of Brahmā that death would come to him from a child.
Remembering this, the destroyer of floods of righteousness, always followed by brave warriors, / quickly went out of his palace with a heart seized by grief.
The Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, terrified and bewildered in mind, / were in haste and astonished in mind among their own ranks.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, the leader of the Dānavas, said: / "It would be a cause of shame for me to flee from this child.
Alas, if I go, he too is taking refuge on a lotus; / and having killed this boy, I would become unapproachable without cause.
Go, run, seize [him], deploy the army!" / Seeing Kumāra, Tāraka, terrible in appearance, said:
"Why, O child, do you wish to fight as if playing with a ball, / [you] whose penance was abandoned, proclaiming a righteous battle?
Because of childhood, your mind sees only small matters." / Kumāra also spoke to him standing before him with the greatest joy:
"Listen, Tāraka: the meaning of the scriptures is not determined here [in battle]. / Objectives are not seen by weapons in battle fraught with terror.
Do not despise my childhood: even a young serpent is dangerous; / the young sun is difficult to look upon; likewise, though a child, I am invincible.
O Daitya, is not a mantra of few syllables seen to be effective?" / While Kumāra was speaking thus, the Daitya hurled a club.
Kumāra repelled that fierce [club] with his discus of unfailing radiance. / Then the lord of the Daityas hurled an iron spear.
And Kārttikeya, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, caught it with his hand. / Rising up, he hurled a loud-sounding mace at the Daitya.
Struck by it, the Daitya then shook like the king of mountains; / then the Daitya deemed the child invincible and very difficult to withstand.
He reflected in his mind: "The appointed time has indeed arrived, there is no doubt." / And seeing him trembling, the foremost Daitya chiefs led by Kālanemi,
all struck Kumāra, who was terrible in battle. / Untouched by those blows and similarly unaffected by afflictions, the one of great splendour,
that child fought in the battle with mighty rushes against the Dānavas. / And the Daitya lords, skilled in battle, struck Kumāra again with arrows,
the mighty Daityas, the thorns of the gods, [struck him] in the battle; / but there was no pain for Kumāra when struck by the weapons of the Daityas.
The battle with the Dānavas became life-ending for the gods. / Seeing the gods tormented, Kumāra was seized with rage.
Then he tore through the army of the Dānavas with weapons. / Struck by those irresistible weapons, the thorns of the gods,
all headed by Kālanemi, indeed turned their backs in battle. / When the Daityas fled and were struck down on all sides,
and [Kumāra's] mind was bewildered by laughter and songs pouring forth from Kinnaras, / [Tāraka] struck Kumāra with a mace glowing like refined gold,
and with variegated arrows he caused the peacock to turn away in battle. / Seeing his mount turned away and shedding blood,
the six-faced god took up in battle a spotless spear adorned with gold, / with his arm brilliant with a golden armlet.
Then Mahāsena said to Tāraka, the lord of the Dānavas: / "Stand, stand, O evil-minded one! Look upon the realm of Yama!
You are indeed slain by me with my spear; remember your Daitya deeds!" / Having spoken thus, he then hurled the spear at the son of Diti.
Released from the arm of Kumāra, accompanied by the sound of his armlet, / it pierced the heart of the Daitya, which was hard as Indra's thunderbolt and mountain.
Lifeless, he fell to the earth like a mountain at the dissolution of the world, / his crown and turban scattered, all his ornaments dropped away.
When that Daitya, the foremost leader of the Dānavas, was slain, / no one was sorrowful then, not even an evildoer in the hells.
Praising the Six-faced One, the gods rejoiced with smiles returning; / they went to their own realms, having cast off grief, filled with joy.
And all the gods, along with the Siddhas rich in penance, / satisfied and having attained all their goals, granted boons to the Six-faced One.
The gods said: / "Whatever wise person reads, hears, or recites / this story concerning Skanda, that man shall become renowned."
Long-lived, fortunate, prosperous, renowned, handsome in appearance, / fearless toward created beings, and free from all sorrow.
Whoever, having observed the morning twilight prayer, recites the deed of Skanda, / accompanied by all the Kinnaras, will become a master of great wealth.
